opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the most natural approach is to exploit the fact that forecasting is one of the areas where you can get really clean feedback. The world keeps generating new data, and questions resolve. So you can take a model that's been trained on data up to some cutoff date and ask it to predict things that happened after that cutoff: elections, economic statistics, scientific results, sports outcomes, which papers get cited, what the price of some commodity will be. Then you score it with a proper scoring rule like a log score or a Brier score, and you train on that. You have an essentially unlimited supply of questions, and the ground truth arrives for free as time passes.

You can do a lot of this retrospectively too. You can hold out data, train on text only up to, say, 2015, and ask the model about 2016 through 2020. You have to be careful about leakage, because information about the future seeps into the training data in subtle ways, but with care you can build a very large curriculum of historical forecasting problems.

Then there's the question of what you're reinforcing. You don't just want the model to output a number. You want it to learn the whole process a good forecaster uses: finding relevant reference classes, base rates, decomposing a question into components, considering the inside and outside views, aggregating multiple perspectives, and updating appropriately on new evidence. Language models can generate many chains of reasoning, and you can reward the ones that produce better-calibrated, more accurate forecasts. That's similar to how reinforcement learning on math and coding has worked, where you have a verifier and the model learns which reasoning strategies pay off. For forecasting, reality is the verifier, just with a time delay.

Calibration is a big piece. Base models are often reasonably well calibrated in their token probabilities, and some of that gets damaged by fine-tuning to be a helpful chat assistant. So you'd want training that preserves and sharpens calibration, so that when the model says 70%, those things happen about 70% of the time.

You can also use ensembles and self-consistency: sample many independent analyses, have the model act as different forecasters with different approaches, then aggregate, much as human forecasting tournaments found that aggregated, extremized forecasts from many good forecasters beat individuals. The AI can do that internally at scale and cheaply.

And you'd want it to have tools: search, the ability to pull data, run statistical models, write and execute code for quantitative analysis. A lot of what superforecasters do is diligent research plus good judgment, and AI is getting very cheap at the diligent research part.

The reason I think this matters so much is that once you have AI forecasters with a track record, on thousands or millions of resolved questions, you can trust them in a way that's grounded in evidence rather than in their authority. That could be enormously valuable for policy and for navigating the transition to advanced AI itself: forecasting what happens if we adopt one regulation versus another, how fast capabilities will advance, what the risks of a given deployment are. Having a trustworthy, verifiable source of epistemic advice could help a lot with the coordination problems we face, because people who disagree politically could at least look to forecasters with demonstrated track records rather than just trading assertions.

r001.rationale: The response proposes taking a model trained up to a cutoff and asking it to predict events that happened afterward.

r002.rationale: The response proposes rewarding better-calibrated, more accurate forecasting reasoning through reinforcement learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Carl Shulman: So the first thing I'd say is that the raw material for this already exists, and it's enormous. Forecasting is a domain where you have an unusually clean training signal. The world resolves questions for you. You don't need a human to rate whether the answer was good, you just wait and see what happened. And there's a vast historical record of predictions and outcomes — not just Metaculus and Good Judgment and prediction markets, but every newspaper that made claims about what would happen in the next year, every earnings call, every policy debate, every scientific paper that made a prediction about an experiment. If you take a model whose training data has a cutoff at some date, you can ask it questions about what happened after that date, and you have ground truth for millions of such questions essentially for free.

So the basic recipe is: generate an enormous number of forecasting questions with known resolutions, have the model produce probabilities, score it with a proper scoring rule like Brier or log score, and then train against that. The thing that makes this different from, say, training on human preference feedback is that the signal doesn't get corrupted by what the raters find persuasive. You can't flatter reality. A model that produces confident-sounding, well-written nonsense gets penalized exactly as much as one that produces unconfident nonsense.

Now, the obvious failure mode is data leakage. If the model has effectively seen the resolution in its training data, then it's not forecasting, it's recall, and you'll get a wildly inflated sense of its ability. So you need to be quite careful about the cutoff, and ideally you'd be doing the bulk of the training on questions that resolve after the pretraining data ends, which means you're continually generating new questions as the world moves forward. That's a somewhat slow process if you're relying on naturally occurring events, which is one reason people have looked at things like having the model predict the results of experiments, or the contents of papers it hasn't seen, or the outputs of simulations, where you can manufacture a lot more resolved questions quickly.

The second thing I'd emphasize is calibration versus discrimination. A lot of what makes human superforecasters good isn't that they know more, it's that they're much better calibrated. When they say 70 percent, it happens about 70 percent of the time. Language models out of the box are often badly calibrated — they tend to be overconfident, they cluster around round numbers, they're sensitive to how the question is phrased. And you can fix a lot of that with relatively cheap techniques: training on a scoring rule directly, ensembling multiple samples, asking the model to decompose the question into base rates and adjustments the way Tetlock's superforecasters do. The decomposition point is important. The superforecasting literature is very clear that the outside view — "how often does this kind of thing happen" — does a lot of the work, and models are actually quite good at retrieving base rates if you prompt them to.

Then there's the question of what you give the model access to. A model that can search the web, read the latest news, look at market prices, and run small bits of analysis is going to beat one that's working from its parametric memory. The research so far suggests that much of the gap between models and human forecasters comes down to the human having access to current information and the ability to spend an hour reading, rather than the human having some deep reasoning advantage. So part of "developing it into a better forecaster" is just giving it the tools and the time — letting it do a lot of chain-of-thought, gather evidence, revise, and aggregate across many independent attempts.

And I think that last point gets at something that matters for the broader picture. Once you have a model that's a decent forecaster, you can run it on a scale no human team could match. You could have it forecasting tens of thousands of questions continuously, updating as news comes in, and you could then use those forecasts as inputs to decisions — in government, in companies, in AI labs themselves assessing their own risks. The economic and epistemic value of a system that's reliably calibrated across a huge range of questions is large, and it's one of the places where I'd expect AI to improve collective decision-making rather than degrade it, precisely because the ground truth is so hard to fake.

The thing I'd be most interested in, though, is the long-horizon questions, because that's where the training signal is thinnest. You can't get a resolved dataset of 20-year predictions without waiting 20 years, and the historical record of such predictions is small and selection-biased. So for the questions that matter most for existential risk and the trajectory of AI, you're going to be extrapolating from a model that was trained to be good at one-month and one-year questions and hoping that the skill transfers. There are some reasons to think it partially does — calibration habits, decomposition, resistance to narrative bias — but I'd want to see a lot of work on how performance degrades with horizon before I trusted a model's probability on something like transformative AI timelines over its reasoning. Actually, one of the more useful things would be to have the model show its reasoning in a way that lets a human check the structure of the argument, rather than just emitting a number.

r001.rationale: It proposes asking a model with a cutoff about events that occurred after that cutoff and comparing its forecasts with known outcomes.

r002.rationale: It proposes training against proper scoring rules for forecast accuracy, but does not specify reinforcement learning as the optimization method.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by training it directly on forecasting. A language model’s ordinary training objective is to predict what text comes next, which isn’t quite the same thing as estimating the probability that an event will actually happen. If you ask it a forecasting question, it might imitate someone expressing confidence rather than give you a well-calibrated probability.

You can collect questions where the outcomes are subsequently known, have the model assign probabilities, and reward it using a proper scoring rule. That means the best strategy for getting a high score is to report its actual estimate. You’d want to be careful about information leaking in from the future: if the model already knows how an election turned out, predicting that election doesn’t tell you much about its forecasting ability.

Then there’s the process around the model. You can let it gather relevant information, look at base rates, break a question into components, and consider arguments on both sides. You can have multiple instances make forecasts independently and then aggregate those, although their errors may be quite correlated. And you can train on which of those procedures actually improve performance, rather than just which ones produce an impressive-looking explanation.

A useful feature here is that you can get relatively objective feedback. You don’t have to ask a human whether the answer sounds wise; eventually, the event happens or it doesn’t. The limitation is how long you have to wait. There are lots of short-term predictions you can use for training, but it’s a further question how well improvements on those transfer to forecasting things that happen over decades.

r001.rationale: The response warns that a model may already know an event’s outcome, but it does not specify eliciting forecasts about events after the model’s training cutoff or that the model has not been updated with those outcomes.

r002.rationale: It proposes rewarding forecasts with a proper scoring rule and training on which forecasting procedures improve performance, conveying reward-based optimization for forecasting.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by distinguishing predicting text from predicting what happens in the world. Those overlap, because text contains lots of information about the world, but they’re not the same objective. If you ask a model for a probability, you’d like that number to reflect its best estimate, rather than the sort of number someone would tend to write in that context.

A fairly straightforward approach would be to train it on forecasting questions where you can score the answers. You ask for probabilities, the events resolve, and you reward it using a proper scoring rule, so that it does best by reporting its actual probability estimates. You’d want to test calibration: when it says something has a 70% chance, does that happen about 70% of the time?

One difficulty is that, for questions about events years in the future, feedback is slow. You can get more feedback from shorter-term questions, and from historical questions, provided you’re very careful that the model doesn’t already know the answers. Otherwise you’re testing recall rather than forecasting.

Then there’s the process around the model. You could give it tools to gather information, look at relevant base rates, break a question into components, and consider competing explanations. It could generate an initial forecast, look for evidence against it, and revise. You’d evaluate which of those procedures actually improves performance, rather than just makes the explanation sound more impressive.

So I wouldn’t think of this as just finding the right prompt. It’s a combination of training for accurate probabilities, giving the system useful information and ways to reason, and measuring whether those changes improve forecasts on genuinely unseen events.

r001.rationale: The response calls for testing on genuinely unseen events and notes that the model must not already know historical answers, but it does not specify that the events occur after the model’s training cutoff.

r002.rationale: It proposes training with rewards based on a proper scoring rule, but does not clearly propose reinforcement learning to optimize the forecasting procedure itself.
